subject: physics
stem: If force F, acceleration A and time T are chosen as fundamental quantities, then the dimension formula of energy
explanation: Energy = force × length, and length = acceleration × time$^2$ ($L = AT^2$). So $E = [F][A][T^2]$. Writing just $[F][A][T]$ leaves out one power of time.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q81)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: A body travels 100 m in the $n^{th}$ second and 125 m in the $(n+3)^{th}$ second. Then the acceleration of body is
explanation: $s_n = u + a(n-\tfrac12)$. Then $s_{n+3}-s_n = 3a = 25$, so $a = 8.33\ \mathrm{ms^{-2}}$. Dividing 25 by 10 or by another wrong gap gives the other options.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q82)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: The resultant magnitude of two vectors is equal to magnitude of both the vectors separately, then the angle between the two vectors is
explanation: $R^2 = P^2+P^2+2P^2\cos\theta = P^2 \Rightarrow \cos\theta = -\tfrac12$, so $\theta = 120^\circ$. $60^\circ$ is the angle the resultant makes with each vector, not the angle between the two vectors.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q83)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: A ball is projected upwards from the top of a tower with a velocity $50\ ms^{-1}$ making an angle $30^\circ$ with the horizontal. The height of tower is $70\ m$. After how many seconds from the instant of throwing, will the ball reach the ground? $(g = 10\ ms^{-2})$
explanation: Vertical motion: $u_y = 25$ m/s. $-70 = 25t - 5t^2 \Rightarrow t^2-5t-14=0 \Rightarrow t = 7$ s. $5$ s is the time to come back to the level of the tower top, so it ignores the 70 m drop.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q84)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: A bullet fired from a gun is given a force $(600 - 2\times10^5\,t)$ newton, where '$t$' is in second. Force on the bullet becomes zero when it leaves the barrel. The average impulse imparted to the bullet is
explanation: $F=0$ at $t = 3\times10^{-3}$ s. $J=\int_0^t F\,dt = 600t - 10^5t^2 = 1.8-0.9 = 0.9$ Ns. $1.8$ Ns comes from $F_0 t$, which wrongly treats the force as constant.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q85)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: A block of mass '$m$' is placed on a smooth wedge of inclination '$\theta$'. This system is accelerated horizontally so that the block does not slip on the wedge. Then, the force exerted by the wedge on the block will be ($g$ - acceleration due to gravity)
explanation: The block accelerates horizontally, so its vertical forces balance: $N\cos\theta = mg$, giving $N = mg/\cos\theta$. $mg\cos\theta$ is the normal force on a wedge that is not accelerating.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q86)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: A block of mass 0.18 kg is attached to a spring of constant $2\ \mathrm{Nm^{-1}}$, the other end of the spring being fixed to a wall; the block rests on a horizontal surface. The coefficient of friction between block and horizontal surface is 0.1. Initially block is at rest and spring is unstretched. When an impulse is given to the block, it slides through a distance 0.06 m and stops. The velocity of the block just after the impulse is given to it is (Take $g = 10\ \mathrm{ms^{-2}}$)
explanation: $\tfrac12mv^2 = \tfrac12kx^2 + \mu mgx = 0.0036 + 0.0108 = 0.0144$ J. So $v^2 = 0.16$ and $v = 0.4$ m/s. Ignoring the spring energy or the friction gives a smaller value.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q87)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: A light inextensible string connects two masses, 0.36 kg and 0.72 kg, hanging on either side of a fixed smooth pulley. The workdone by the string on mass 0.36 kg during first second after the masses are released (Take $g = 10\ \mathrm{ms^{-2}}$)
explanation: $a = \frac{0.36}{1.08}g = \frac{10}{3}\ \mathrm{ms^{-2}}$ and $T = \frac{2m_1m_2g}{m_1+m_2} = 4.8$ N. Distance in 1 s is $\tfrac12at^2 = \tfrac53$ m. $W = 4.8\times\tfrac53 = 8$ J (positive, since the lighter mass moves up). Using $mg$ instead of $T$ gives 6 J.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q88)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: Two particles A and B initially at rest move towards each other under a mutual force of attraction. At the instant, the speed of A is V and the speed of B is 2V, find the speed of centre of mass of the system, if the masses of A and B are in the ratio of 2 : 1
explanation: Only internal forces act, so momentum stays zero. Check: $2m\cdot V - m\cdot 2V = 0$, so $v_{cm}=0$. The non-zero options add the speeds without accounting for their opposite directions.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q89)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: Two Simple Harmonic Motions are given by $y_1 = A\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}t+\phi\right)$ and $y_2 = B\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}t+\phi\right)$. The phase difference between these two after one sec is
explanation: $\Delta\varphi = \left(\frac{2\pi}{3}-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)t = \frac{\pi}{6}$ at $t = 1$ s. The initial phases cancel. The other options use a single angular frequency on its own instead of the difference.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q91)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: A block of mass 1 kg is dropped on a spring-mass system: a 3 kg mass rests on a vertical spring fixed to the ground. The block travels 100 m in the air before striking the 3 kg mass. Calculate the maximum compression in the spring, if both the blocks move together after the collision (Spring constant of the spring, $k = 1.25\times10^6$ N/m, $g = 10\ \mathrm{ms^{-2}}$)
explanation: Impact speed $v=\sqrt{2000}$ m/s. Perfectly inelastic collision: $V = v/4$, so KE $= \tfrac12(4)V^2 = 250$ J. Gravity and the initial compression are negligible because $k$ is huge: $\tfrac12kx^2 \approx 250 \Rightarrow x = 0.02$ m = 2 cm. Using the 1 kg block's KE before the collision (1000 J) gives 4 cm, which ignores the energy lost in the collision.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q92)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: The weight of a body decreases by 1% when it is raised to a small height 'h' above the earth's surface. If the same body is taken to a depth 'h' in a mine, then its weight is
explanation: Height: $\Delta g/g = 2h/R = 1\%$. Depth: $\Delta g/g = h/R = 0.5\%$, also a decrease. Weight increases with neither height nor depth.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q93)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: A spring is stretched by applying a load to its free end. The strain produced in the spring is
explanation: When a helical spring is stretched, its overall length changes (longitudinal strain) and the coiled wire twists (shear strain), so both are produced. The shape and volume of the wire hardly change, so volumetric strain is negligible.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q94)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: When a body floats in water and another liquid separately, it floats with one third of its volume outside water and $\frac{3}{4}$ of its volume outside another liquid. The density of the liquid is
explanation: In water, $\tfrac23$ is submerged, so $\rho_b = \tfrac23$ g/cc. In the liquid, $\tfrac14$ is submerged: $\rho_l\cdot\tfrac14 = \tfrac23 \Rightarrow \rho_l = \tfrac83$ g/cc. $\tfrac38$ is the reciprocal, from inverting the ratio.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q95)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: Two rods A and B of lengths in ratio of 1 : 2 have thermal conductivities in 1 : 2 ratio and cross sectional areas in 1 : 4 ratio. The temperature difference between the ends of two rods is same. Then the ratio of heat currents is $(H_A : H_B)$
explanation: $H \propto KA/L$. $H_A:H_B = \frac{1\cdot1}{1} : \frac{2\cdot4}{2} = 1:4$. 4 : 1 is the same ratio inverted.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q97)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: An electric heater supplies heat to a system at a rate of 100 W. If system performs work at rate of 75 joules per second. The rate of increase of internal energy is
explanation: $dU/dt = dQ/dt - dW/dt = 100 - 75 = 25$ J/s. Adding the work gives 175 J/s, which comes from the wrong sign convention.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q98)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: A Carnot heat engine receives 300 J of heat from the source and rejects 150 J to sink. If source and sink are at $227^\circ$C and T K, then T is
explanation: $Q_2/Q_1 = T_2/T_1 \Rightarrow T = 500\times\frac{150}{300} = 250$ K. Using $227$ instead of $500$ K gives a wrong result, because the source temperature must be in kelvin.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q99)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: The Mean free path of a gas molecule, whose diameter is $2\times10^{-10}$ m is $1.6\times10^{-7}$ m. Calculate the mean free path of another gas molecule whose diameter is $4\times10^{-10}$ m (under the same conditions)
explanation: $\lambda \propto 1/d^2$. Doubling $d$ divides $\lambda$ by 4: $1.6\times10^{-7}/4 = 0.4\times10^{-7}$ m. $0.8\times10^{-7}$ m assumes $\lambda \propto 1/d$.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q100)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: Ten tuning forks are arranged in increasing order of frequency. Any two nearest tuning forks produce 4 beats per second. The highest frequency of tuning fork is twice that of the lowest possible, then the highest and lowest frequencies, in Hz, are respectively
explanation: There are 9 gaps: $f_{max} = f_{min} + 36 = 2f_{min} \Rightarrow f_{min} = 36$ and $f_{max} = 72$ Hz. Counting 10 gaps gives 80 and 40.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q101)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: A glass slab has a critical angle of $30^\circ$ when placed in air. What will be the critical angle when it is placed in a liquid of refractive index 6/5? $\left(\sin 53^\circ = \frac{4}{5}\right)$
explanation: $\mu_g = 1/\sin30^\circ = 2$. In the liquid, $\sin C = \frac{6/5}{2} = \frac35 \Rightarrow C = 37^\circ$. $53^\circ$ is the complementary angle ($\sin = 4/5$).

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q102)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: An object is placed at 10 cm from a lens and a real image is formed with magnification of 0.5. The lens is

options.text: Concave with focal length of $\frac{10}{3}$ cm
Convex with focal length of $\frac{10}{3}$ cm
Concave with focal length of 10 cm
Convex with focal length of 10 cm

explanation: A real image requires a convex lens. $m = -0.5$, $u=-10$ cm, so $v = +5$ cm. $\frac1f = \frac15 + \frac1{10} = \frac3{10}$, giving $f = \frac{10}{3}$ cm. A concave lens always forms virtual images.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q103)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: Two point charges $Q$ and $-4Q$ are separated by a distance $r$. If electric field at the location of $Q$ is $\vec{E}$, then the field at the location of $-4Q$ is
explanation: At $Q$, the field due to $-4Q$ has magnitude $4kQ/r^2$ and points toward $-4Q$. At $-4Q$, the field due to $Q$ has magnitude $kQ/r^2$ and points away from $Q$, which is the same direction. So it equals $\vec E/4$. Choosing $-\vec E/4$ assumes the field reverses, as Newton's third law does for forces.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q105)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: When three parallel plate capacitors A, B and C are connected in series, the effective capacitance is $10\ \mu$F. If the capacitor C of capacitance $30\ \mu$F is removed from the combination, the effective capacitance becomes $15\ \mu$F. If the capacitances of A and B are in the ratio 1 : 3, then the energy stored when the three capacitors A, B and C are connected in parallel to a dc supply of 100 V is
explanation: A and B in series give $\frac{3x^2}{4x} = 15 \Rightarrow x = 20$, so A = 20 μF and B = 60 μF. In parallel, $C = 110$ μF and $U = \tfrac12CV^2 = \tfrac12(110\times10^{-6})(10^4) = 0.55$ J = 550 mJ. Forgetting the $\tfrac12$ or dropping C gives the other values.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q106)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: If two positive charges each of $20\ \mu$C are placed at the two vertices of an equilateral triangle of side 50 cm and a third positive charge of $10\sqrt{3}\ \mu$C is placed at the centroid of the triangle, then the electrostatic potential energy of the system of three charges is
explanation: Vertex pair: $9\times10^9\times400\times10^{-12}/0.5 = 7.2$ J. Distance from a vertex to the centroid is $0.5/\sqrt3$ m, so each vertex-centroid pair gives $10.8$ J and the two give $21.6$ J. Total is $28.8$ J. 21.6 J leaves out the vertex-vertex pair.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q107)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: When the current through a battery is 5A, the potential difference across its terminals is 9V and when the current through that battery is 3A, the potential difference across its terminals is 12V. If the same battery is connected to an external resistor of resistance $4\Omega$, then the current through the $4\Omega$ resistor is,
explanation: $E-5r=9$ and $E-3r=12$, so $r=1.5\ \Omega$ and $E=16.5$ V. $I = 16.5/(4+1.5) = 3$ A. Ignoring the internal resistance gives about 4 A.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q108)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: In a potentiometer experiment, the potentiometer wire of length 4m and resistance $20\ \Omega$ is connected in series with an external resistor of resistance $979\ \Omega$ and a cell of internal resistance $1\ \Omega$. If the emf of the cell is 1.2 V, then the length of the wire between two points where the potential difference is 12 mV is
explanation: $I = 1.2/(20+979+1) = 1.2$ mA. Drop across the wire $= 24$ mV, so the gradient is $6$ mV/m. Length $= 12/6 = 2$ m. Leaving out the internal resistance barely changes the result, but leaving out the 979 Ω resistor is a gross error.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q109)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: The current and voltage sensitivities of a moving coil galvanometer are 80 divisions per mA and 2 divisions per mV respectively. If the galvanometer has 100 divisions, then the resistance to be connected in series to the galvanometer to convert it into a voltmeter which can measure a maximum potential difference of 5 V is
explanation: $G = S_I/S_V = 80/2 = 40\ \Omega$ and $I_g = 100/80 = 1.25$ mA. $R = V/I_g - G = 4000 - 40 = 3960\ \Omega$. Adding $G$ instead of subtracting it gives 4040 Ω.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q110)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: A circular coil of radius 10 cm having 200 turns is carrying a current of 2A. If the magnetic field at a point on the axis of the coil which is at a distance of 20 cm from the center of the coil is B, then the magnetic field at a point on the axis which is at a distance of 5 cm from the center of the coil is
explanation: $B \propto (R^2+x^2)^{-3/2}$. Ratio $= \left(\frac{100+400}{100+25}\right)^{3/2} = 4^{3/2} = 8$, so the field is $8B$. 4B comes from forgetting the 3/2 power.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q111)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: A magnetic material placed in a magnetic field of intensity $H = 1000\ Am^{-1}$ has magnetization $M = 2\ Am^{-1}$. The magnetic susceptibility, and type of material is
explanation: $\chi = M/H = 2\times10^{-3}$. It is small and positive, so the material is paramagnetic. Diamagnetic materials have negative $\chi$, and ferromagnetic materials have $\chi \gg 1$.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q112)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: In a coil of resistance $10\Omega$, the induced current developed by changing magnetic flux through it decreases linearly with time from 4 A at $t = 0$ to zero at $t = 0.1$ s. The magnitude of change in flux through the coil in weber is
explanation: Charge = area under the $i$-$t$ graph $= \tfrac12\times4\times0.1 = 0.2$ C. Since $q = \Delta\Phi/R$, $\Delta\Phi = 0.2\times10 = 2$ Wb. Leaving out the $\tfrac12$ of the triangle gives 4 Wb.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q113)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: In a series LCR circuit driven by an ac source, three ac voltmeters are connected: $V_1$ across the resistor R, $V_2$ across the series combination of inductor L and capacitor C, and $V_3$ across the source. At resonance,
explanation: At resonance $V_L = V_C$ and they are $180^\circ$ out of phase, so the voltage across the L-C pair is zero: $V_2 = 0$. The whole source voltage appears across R, so $V_1 = V_3 \neq 0$.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q114)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: About 5% of the power of a 100 $W$ light bulb is converted to visible radiation. Then the average intensity of visible radiation at a distance of 1 $m$ from the bulb is approximately (Assume that the radiation is emitted isotropically and neglect reflection)
explanation: $I = P/(4\pi r^2) = 5/(4\pi) \approx 0.4\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$. Using a hemisphere ($2\pi r^2$) gives about 0.8, and other area mistakes give 0.2 or 0.6.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q115)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: When a metal surface is illuminated with lights of wavelengths $\lambda$ and $2\lambda$ separately, the stopping potentials are $V$ and $\frac{V}{3}$ respectively. Then the threshold wavelength of that metal surface is
explanation: $\frac{hc}{\lambda}-\phi = eV$ and $\frac{hc}{2\lambda}-\phi = \frac{eV}{3}$. Subtracting gives $eV = \frac{3hc}{4\lambda}$, so $\phi = \frac{hc}{4\lambda}$ and $\lambda_0 = 4\lambda$. Small algebra slips lead to $6\lambda$ or $\frac{8\lambda}{3}$.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q116)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: The minimum frequency of light which can ionize a hydrogen atom is approximately
explanation: $\nu = \frac{13.6\times1.6\times10^{-19}}{6.63\times10^{-34}} \approx 3.3\times10^{15}$ Hz. 91.1 is the series-limit wavelength in nm, not a frequency.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q117)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: The activities of a sample of radioactive material are $A_1$ and $A_2$ at times $t_1$ and $t_2$ respectively $(t_2 > t_1)$. If its mean life time is $T$, then
explanation: $A = A_0e^{-\lambda t}$ with $\lambda = 1/T$, so $A_2 = A_1e^{-(t_2-t_1)/T}$. Option 1 would mean the activity grows. Options 3 and 4 multiply by $T$ when they should divide by it.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q118)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: Two amplifiers are connected one after the other in series (cascaded). Their voltage gains are 10 and 20 respectively. If the input ac signal is 0.01 volt, the output ac signal is
explanation: In a cascade the gains multiply: $10\times20 = 200$, so the output is $0.01\times200 = 2$ V. Adding the gains (30) gives 0.3 V, and 0.03 V comes from a similar slip.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 13 May Shift 2, Q119)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: A carrier wave of peak voltage 12 $V$ is used to transit a message signal. If the modulation index is 75 %, then the peak voltage of the modulating signal is
explanation: $\mu = A_m/A_c \Rightarrow A_m = 0.75\times12 = 9$ V. 16 V comes from dividing ($12/0.75$) instead of multiplying.

source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice
